html:
Mennonites have farmed the Paraguayan Chaco since 1927, when German-speaking settlers from Canada founded the Menno Colony. Others came from the Soviet Union in 1930 and after the Second World War.

A law of 1921 promised these Protestant pacifists freedom from military service and their own schools, and Paraguay wanted settlers to hold the Chaco against Bolivia. The first years in the hot, dry scrub were hard, and many died. Their colonies lay near the front of the Chaco War and supplied the Paraguayan army.

Around Filadelfia they built cooperatives that became leaders in dairy and beef. Like the Mennonites in Belize, they kept their language and faith and became important farmers. Their success came partly at the expense of the Indigenous peoples of the Chaco, who lost their land.
sum: Mennonites have farmed the Paraguayan Chaco since 1927, when German-speaking settlers from Canada founded the Menno Colony. Others came from the Soviet Union in 1930 and after the Second World War.
